newsitem.title: USA: Debate over aspartame resumes in medical journal.
newsitem.headline: Debate over aspartame resumes in medical journal.

text.p: A professor of psychiatry who has been an ardent opponent of aspartame since the artificial sweetener was introduced in 1981 has cited a slightly higher incidence of brain tumors as a reason for further study.

"Compared to other environmental factors, aspartame appears to be a promising candidate for explaining the surge in brain tumors in the mid-1980s," John Olney of Washington University in St. Louis wrote in the Journal of Neuropathology and Experimental Neurology.

Citing statistics on cancerous brain tumors from the U.S. National Cancer Institute and an animal study suggesting a link, he concluded that the popular sweetener may have played a role in the mid-1980s rise in brain tumors to an average of 53 per million people from 48 per million in the 1970s. He said similar increases in tumors have appeared in Europe.

The FDA has received complaints that aspartame causes adverse effects including headaches and nausea. People suffering from phenylketonuria, a congenital condition that can cause mental retardation, have been told not to use products containing aspartame.

Aspartame is made up of amino acids much sweeter than sugar but has not been shown to aid dieters appreciably in losing weight. Manufacturers of aspartame, sold under the brand name NutraSweet, strongly criticized the report, which was published Friday, and said the data had been manipulated.
Such reports could hit sales of thousands of food and drink items that use the low-calorie sweetener.

Olney said other risk factors common to industrialized nations such as higher levels of ionizing radiation, smoke in the air, pesticides, industrial chemicals and electromagnetic fields could be responsible for rising tumor rates. But he cited "the need for a reassessment of the carcinogenic (cancer-causing) potential of this agent, which is currently being ingested throughout many parts of the world."

NutraSweet Kelco Co. of Chicago, a unit of Monsanto Co., which makes the sweetener and held the patent until it expired in 1992, said brain cancer rates were increasing before aspartame was approved for sale by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 1981.

"The incidence of brain cancer is a gradual long-term trend that started well before aspartame was first marketed and the rate of increase actually slowed down after aspartame came into widespread use," spokesman Richard Nelson said.

Nelson argued that Olney excluded data from 1973 and 1974, when brain cancer rates were comparatively low. If included, the data would show brain cancer rates were rising before aspartame reached the market in 1981, he said.
Through a spokesman at Washington University, Olney said on Monday he would rather have the debate play out in scientific journals and not in the media and would not respond directly to questions.
